# What is agentkit and what is it built on?

**agentkit** is a shared, self-hosted, multi-tenant agent platform for organizations with many product teams, serving several tenants without a managed agent runtime [1]. It lets teams build agents in a uniform way: an agent is described declaratively in `agent.yaml`, picking a model, prompt, tools, skills, subagents and middleware by name from shared pools [2]. Phase 0 is complete — a deep-research agent defined in YAML and built through the `build_deep_agent` factory runs end to end on any of six registry models, with persisted threads, tenant-tagged traces, a usage ledger, and each tenant getting its own stamped deployment (database, AES key, collector, ports) [1][3].

## What it is built on

agentkit is built on three core technologies, pinned at specific versions [1]:

- **DeepAgents** (`deepagents==0.7.32`)
- **LangChain v1** (`langchain==1.4.7`)
- **LangGraph** (`langgraph==1.2.19`)

Architecturally, agentkit is a **thin policy layer over DeepAgents, not a fork** [2]. The `build_deep_agent` factory in `agentkit-deep` is the single place that calls DeepAgents' `create_deep_agent`; it always adds the `PlatformContext` schema, puts `TenantGuardMiddleware` first, and wires encrypted Postgres persistence and memory tiers when asked [2]. Around this core, the platform is organized into packages: `agentkit-core` (Settings, model registry, `PlatformContext`), `agentkit-config` (validation and resolution of `agent.yaml`), `agentkit-middleware` (tenant guard, selection middleware, retry/circuit breaker), `agentkit-tools` (e.g. `web_search`, `fetch_url`), `agentkit-persistence` (encrypted Postgres per tenant), `agentkit-telemetry` (OTLP traces + usage ledger), and `agentkit-evals` (citation checks + LLM judge) [2][4].

## Sources

[2] https://github.com/cwijayasundara/deep_agents_fw_v1.0/blob/main/README.md

# `build_deep_agent`: what it does and why it is the single entry point to DeepAgents

## What it does

`build_deep_agent` is the factory in `packages/agentkit-deep/src/agentkit_deep/factory.py` that turns
declarative configuration into a runnable agent. It takes keyword-only arguments — `model`,
`system_prompt`, `tools`, `subagents`, `middleware`, `settings`, `checkpointer`, `name`, `skills`,
`backend`, `permissions`, `store`, `persistence` — and returns a compiled graph [1]. It is the only
caller of DeepAgents' `create_deep_agent` [1][2].

Whatever the caller passes, the factory always enforces the following [3][4]:

- **A concrete model** — `model` must be a `BaseChatModel` or a `ModelSpec`; a `ModelSpec` needs
  `settings` and is built with `get_model`, which fails fast if the provider key is missing [3].
- **`context_schema=PlatformContext`** — every run must pass `context=PlatformContext(...)` (a dict is
  validated against the schema) [3][4].
- **`TenantGuardMiddleware` first** — the guard for the deployment tenant (`settings.deployment_tenant`,
  or `AGENTKIT_TENANT` read once per process when no settings are given) is prepended to the caller's
  middleware; passing your own `TenantGuardMiddleware` raises `ValueError` [3]. The guard rejects runs
  with no `PlatformContext` (`MissingPlatformContext`) or a mismatched tenant (`TenantMismatch`) [5].
- **Caller middleware order preserved** — the list is `[guard, *middleware]`; when built from YAML the
  middleware is sorted into a canonical order (`selection`, `model_fallback`, `model_retry`,
  `tool_retry`, `require_output`, `call_limit`, `tool_call_limit`, `pii`, then other pool entries), so
  file order no longer matters and resilience wrappers nest correctly [3].
- **Skills** — `skills` are skill *sources* (`skills_source(owner)`), passed through with `backend` and
  `permissions`, giving each owner a read-only skills view [4][6].
- **Persistence** — with `persistence`, its encrypted `saver` and `store` become the checkpointer and
  store (passing `checkpointer` or `store` too raises `ValueError`); the backend becomes
  `memory_backend()` unless the caller passed one built by `memory_backend(...)`;
  `memory=["/org/AGENTS.md", "/memories/AGENTS.md"]`; and `ORG_WRITE_DENY` is prepended to the
  permissions [4].
- **Prompt hash** — the returned graph is
  `agent.with_config(metadata={"prompt_hash": prompt_hash(system_prompt)})`, the SHA-256 hex of the
  prompt text, so every run and trace inherits it [4].

## Why it is the single entry point

It is the platform's deliberate choke point — the design principle that agentkit is "a thin, opinionated
policy layer over DeepAgents, not a fork." `build_deep_agent` is the one place that calls
`deepagents.create_deep_agent`; it adds all platform policy (tenant guard, context schema, memory
routes, permissions, prompt hash) through the SDK's own extension points — `context_schema`, the
user-middleware slot, `CompositeBackend` routes and `FilesystemPermission` — so no upstream code is
patched or vendored [2][4]. Because every agent is funneled through this one factory, the same policy
guarantees hold no matter what the caller passes [3].

It also anchors the declarative workflow: teams describe an agent in `agent.yaml`, picking a model,
prompt, tools, skills, subagents and middleware by name from shared pools; `agentkit-config` validates
every name at load time and resolves the file into kwargs for `build_deep_agent` [2][4]. The pipeline is
`agent.yaml` → `agentkit-config` (load, validate, resolve) → `build_deep_agent` (TenantGuard first,
memory tiers, prompt hash) → DeepAgents `create_deep_agent` → run with `context=PlatformContext` [2].

One related caveat the docs note: because the tenant guard runs inside the graph (after LangGraph has
checkpointed the input), any code that invokes a persistent graph directly must make the tenant check
itself — this requirement is documented on `build_deep_agent` and `load_flow` [7]. The architecture doc
also flags a gap: the factory does not yet disable DeepAgents' automatically added `general-purpose`
subagent [3].

# What goes in `agent.yaml` and where the names come from

## What a team can put in `agent.yaml`

An `agent.yaml` is a declarative spec (`apiVersion: agentkit/v1`, `kind: Agent`) that `agentkit-config` compiles into a graph. Specs are pydantic models with `extra="forbid"`, so any key not listed below is a load error [1]. The full field set is [2]:

| Field | Type, default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `apiVersion` | `"agentkit/v1"` (required) | Format version |
| `kind` | `"Agent"` (required) | |
| `name` | str (required) | Becomes `PlatformContext.agent_name`; must be a valid label |
| `description` | str, `""` | |
| `version` | str, `"0.1.0"` | Becomes `PlatformContext.agent_version` |
| `tags` | list of str, `[]` | |
| `model` | str (required) | Entry name in `models.yaml` |
| `tier` | str, `"default"` | `fast`, `default` or `strong` |
| `selection` | `decisions` or null | Decisions picks visible tools and the tier |
| `prompt` | str (required) | Prompt pool name, e.g. `research/orchestrator` |
| `tools` | list of tool refs, `[]` | e.g. `web_search`, or `{fetch_url: {max_chars: 20000}}`, or `{name: ..., params: {...}}` |
| `skills` | list of str, `[]` | Skill pool names |
| `subagents` | list, `[]` | Each entry is a subagent pool name or an inline `SubAgentSpec` (same shape as a subagent file: `name`, `description`, `prompt`, `tools`) [3] |
| `middleware` | list of `{type, params, enabled}`, `[]` | Middleware pool entries; `enabled: false` skips one |
| `output` | str or null | Absolute path of the file holding the agent's answer (e.g. `/report.md`); null means the last AI message |

The shipped example, `apps/research_agent/agent.yaml`, wires a `research_agent` with `model: fireworks-glm`, tier `default`, Decisions selection, the `research/orchestrator` prompt, `web_search`/`fetch_url` tools, a `researcher` subagent plus an inline `critic`, and middleware such as `model_fallback`, `model_retry`, `call_limit`, per-tool `tool_call_limit`s, PII guards and `require_output` [4][5].

Names are checked at load time, before any key lookup or network call: unknown model entry or tier, unknown prompt, unknown tool (or bad params, or duplicates), unknown skill, unknown middleware type, and unknown/duplicate subagents all become `SpecError`s [6].

## Where the names come from

Pools resolve the names used in the YAML to objects. File pools come from library roots (e.g. `libraries/`); code pools come from package entry points [7]:

- **Prompts** — `<root>/prompts/**/*.md`; the name is the path under `prompts/` without `.md` (so `research/orchestrator`) [7].
- **Skills** — `<root>/skills/*/SKILL.md`; the name is the directory name, which must equal the front matter `name` [7].
- **Subagents** — `<root>/subagents/*.yaml`; the name is the file's `name` field (e.g. `researcher` from `libraries/subagents/researcher.yaml`) [7][3].
- **Agents** — `<root>/agents/*.yaml` and `<root>/agent.yaml`; the name is the file's `name`, resolving to the file path for flow agent nodes [7].
- **Tools and middleware** — entry point groups `agentkit.tools` and `agentkit.middleware` declared in each package's `pyproject.toml` (e.g. `web_search`, `fetch_url`, `call_limit`); the name is the entry point name, resolving to a factory [7][8].
- **Models** — entries in `packages/agentkit-core/src/agentkit_core/models.yaml` (e.g. `openai`, `anthropic`, `fireworks-glm`), which map a logical entry name to a provider model id per tier [7][9].

# Checking agent YAML files before running them

## The command

Run `uv run agentkit validate <files>` to check your YAML before committing or running it [1][2]. The validator handles all three file kinds — `kind: Agent`, `kind: SubAgent` and `kind: Flow` — detecting the kind from the file itself, and works fully offline [3]. For example, validating a single agent looks like `uv run agentkit validate path/to/agent.yaml` [2].

To check everything at once, `make lint` validates every shipped agent, flow and subagent with:

```bash
uv run agentkit validate apps/*/agent.yaml apps/*/flows/*.yaml libraries/subagents/*.yaml
```

It prints each problem, then a summary line `checked N file(s): E error(s), W warning(s)`, and exits 1 on any error [4].

## Exit codes

`agentkit validate PATH...` exits 0 when there are no errors (warnings are allowed), 1 on errors, and 2 on bad usage; unmatched shell globs are skipped [3].

## What validation catches

Validation happens at load time, before any key lookup or network call. The checks cover [5]:

- Unknown keys anywhere, a wrong `kind` or `apiVersion`, YAML syntax errors, empty files, and non-UTF-8 files
- Unknown model entry or tier (errors list the known names)
- Unknown prompts, or a prompt using a variable other than `agent_name` and `date`
- Unknown tools, duplicate tools in one list, or params the factory signature does not accept
- Unknown skills, or a skill whose `SKILL.md` names tools the owning agent or subagent lacks (DeepAgents built-in tools always count as owned)
- Unknown middleware types or bad params (`type: selection` is rejected — use top-level `selection:`)
- Unknown or duplicate subagents, or a subagent named like its parent
- Unknown `response_schema`; a subagent with no `response_schema` gets the warning `no response_schema; completion contract recommended`
- An `output` that is not an absolute path

Problems are reported as `SpecError(file, path, message, severity)` records, with paths in YAML notation such as `subagents[0].tools[1]`; the underlying `validate_agent`/`validate_subagent`/`validate_flow` functions never raise — they return every problem they find [5].

## Notes and limits

- Missing API keys are **not** validation errors, so `agentkit validate` runs in CI without secrets; missing keys fail later at build time with a `ConfigError` naming the variable [4].
- After a file validates, run the agent with `research --agent path/to/agent.yaml`, or via `load_agent` from your own entry point; to make it usable from flows, place it where the agents pool finds it (`<root>/agent.yaml` or `<root>/agents/*.yaml`) [2].

# When does a missing API key cause a failure, and does `agentkit validate` catch it?

**Short answer:** `agentkit validate` does **not** catch missing API keys — that is by design. The failure happens later, **at build time**, when a `ConfigError` is raised naming the missing environment variable [1].

## Details

- **Validation is secret-free by design.** Missing API keys are explicitly *not* validation errors, which is what allows `agentkit validate` to run in CI without any secrets present. `make lint` therefore runs `uv run agentkit validate apps/*/agent.yaml apps/*/flows/*.yaml libraries/subagents/*.yaml` with no keys configured [1].
- **Where it actually fails:** at build (load) time, with a `ConfigError` whose message names the missing variable — e.g. the shipped `research_agent` needs `OPENAI_API_KEY`, the provider's own key, and `FIREWORKS_API_KEY` for its fallback model [1][2].
- **Validation checks happen before any key lookup.** The validator's checklist (unknown keys, wrong `kind`/`apiVersion`, unknown models/tiers, unknown tools or skills, middleware problems, etc.) is checked "at load time, before any key lookup or network call," confirming key presence is outside its scope [3].
- **Related nuance:** in the live provider tests (`pytest -m live ...test_live_providers.py`), a registry entry whose key is missing is *skipped*, not failed — one short call per registry entry [4]. And you can avoid needing an OpenAI key at runtime by passing `--no-selection`, though a Fireworks key is still required for the fallback model [2].

# Running the research agent and switching its model provider

## 1. Set up

1. Copy the environment template and fill in the keys you have: `cp .env.example .env` (`.env` is git-ignored; keys are searched from the nearest `.env` upward from your current directory, and `.env` values win over shell exports) [1][2].
2. Optionally verify the install: `make test` (uv sync pinned via `constraints.txt` plus offline tests) and `make lint` [1].

## 2. Run it

```bash
UV_CONSTRAINT=constraints.txt uv run research "your question"
UV_CONSTRAINT=constraints.txt uv run research-eval --judge anthropic   # evals
```

[1]

Key facts about a run:

- The agent is defined in `apps/research_agent/agent.yaml`; `--agent <file>` runs a different agent file [1][3].
- Both CLIs share agent options from `research_agent.agent.add_agent_args`: `--agent PATH`, `--model ENTRY`, `--tier {fast,default,strong}`, `--no-selection`, `--tenant LABEL`, `--user LABEL`, `--persist` (encrypted Postgres threads/memory; needs `DATABASE_URL` and `LANGGRAPH_AES_KEY`), and `-v`/`-q` for logging. `research` also takes `--thread ID` (resume a persisted thread) and `--out PATH` (where the report is written, default `report.md`) [3].
- Both CLIs log progress to stderr (resolved model, keys set, Decisions selection, delegations, searches, fetches, file writes, run time) [1].
- The report is saved to `/report.md` per the agent definition's `output:` key (the CLI's `--out` defaults to `report.md`) [3][4].

## 3. Which API keys you need

| What you run | Keys it needs |
|---|---|
| The shipped `apps/research_agent/agent.yaml` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` (it sets `selection: decisions`), the chosen provider's own key, and `FIREWORKS_API_KEY` for any `--model` (its fallback model `fireworks-glm:strong` is built at load) |
| Any run with `--no-selection` | The provider's own key plus `FIREWORKS_API_KEY` |
| `research-eval` | The above, plus the `--judge` entry's key (default `anthropic`) |

[2][5]

Web search uses DuckDuckGo and needs no key; for Tavily instead, set `tools: [{web_search: {backend: tavily}}, fetch_url]` and `TAVILY_API_KEY` (a subagent's tools replace the parent's, so set the backend on each subagent too) [2].

To try a provider without an OpenAI key, pass `--no-selection`: the agent sees every tool and stays on the configured tier (a Fireworks key is still needed) [2].

## 4. Switching the model provider

Switching provider is a config change, not code: pass `--model <registry entry>` on the CLI, or edit the `model:` key in the agent YAML [6].

```bash
UV_CONSTRAINT=constraints.txt uv run research "your question" --model anthropic
```

The default is `fireworks-glm` (`accounts/fireworks/models/glm-5p3-flash`) [1]. Available registry entries in `models.yaml` [6][7]:

| Entry | Provider | Model id (fast/default) | API key |
|---|---|---|---|
| `openai` | `openai` | `gpt-6-luna` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| `google_genai` | `google_genai` | `gemini-3.8-flash` | `GOOGLE_API_KEY` |
| `anthropic` | `anthropic` | `claude-haiku-5-5` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
| `fireworks-deepseek` | `fireworks` | `accounts/fireworks/models/deepseek-v4p1-flash-1017` | `FIREWORKS_API_KEY` |
| `fireworks-glm` | `fireworks` | `accounts/fireworks/models/glm-5p3-flash` | `FIREWORKS_API_KEY` |
| `fireworks-minimax` | `fireworks` | `accounts/fireworks/models/minimax-m3p1-flash` | `FIREWORKS_API_KEY` |

Tiers: `--tier` picks `fast`, `default`, or `strong`. `fast` and `default` stay on the cheap model; `strong` is a bigger model only for `anthropic` (`claude-opus-5-5`), `fireworks-glm` (`glm-5p3`), and `fireworks-minimax` (`minimax-m3`). `openai`, `google_genai`, and `fireworks-deepseek` have no strong model chosen yet, so tier switching changes nothing on those entries [6].

Under the hood, `ModelRegistry.resolve(name, tier)` returns a `ModelSpec(provider, model_id, kwargs)`, and `get_model` calls `langchain.chat_models.init_chat_model(...)`; the provider must be one of `openai`, `google_genai`, `anthropic`, `fireworks` [6].

## 5. One caveat

The shipped research agent's `model_fallback` target (`fireworks-glm:strong`) is built at load, so `FIREWORKS_API_KEY` is required for every `--model`, not only Fireworks entries. Drop the `model_fallback` middleware entry (or point it at the run's own provider) to run without a Fireworks key. Also note a failing primary model silently switches to the fallback: only the ledger row's `model` field (all model ids called, comma-joined) shows the switch [8][9].

# Middleware stack order in agent.yaml

## Short answer

The order in `agent.yaml` does **not** matter. From YAML, the `middleware` list is sorted into a canonical order (`agentkit_config/stack.py`, `STACK_ORDER`) before the agent is built, so "file order no longer matters" [1][2].

## The canonical order

The factory `build_deep_agent` builds the middleware list as `[guard, *middleware]`, where `TenantGuardMiddleware` is always prepended first (passing your own `TenantGuardMiddleware` raises `ValueError`). From YAML, the rest is then sorted into this canonical `STACK_ORDER` [1][2][3]:

1. `TenantGuardMiddleware` (always first / outermost; added by the factory)
2. `selection` (only when `selection: decisions`)
3. `model_fallback`
4. `model_retry`
5. `tool_retry`
6. `require_output`
7. `call_limit`
8. `tool_call_limit`
9. `pii`
10. then any other pool entries in file order

After this user-middleware slot, DeepAgents wraps its own stack around it [1].

## Why the fixed order matters (wrapping semantics)

The first entry is the outermost wrapper, and each ordering choice is deliberate [1]:

- `SelectionMiddleware` overrides the request's model, so `model_fallback` sits **inside** it and can swap the model on failure.
- `model_retry` sits **inside** `model_fallback`, so each model is retried before the next one is tried.
- `require_output` sits **outside** `call_limit`, so the model calls its nudges cause are counted against the budget.

Because the order is enforced by the config layer, the shipped `apps/research_agent/agent.yaml` can list its middleware in any sequence (model_fallback, model_retry, call_limit, tool_call_limits, pii, require_output) and the same stack results [2][4].

## Related constraint: duplicates, not order

Instead of relying on file order, validation rejects duplicates: a second enabled `selection`, `model_fallback`, `model_retry`, `tool_retry`, `require_output`, or `call_limit`, repeats of `pii` (same `type`), or `tool_call_limit` (same `tool_name`). An agent without an enabled `call_limit` gets a warning [1].

# What does the `require_output` middleware do?

`require_output` is one of the standard Phase 1 middleware in the stack. When the model ends its turn with a plain reply and no tool call before `/report.md` has been written in that run, the middleware sends the run back to the model as a user nudge [1][2]. The nudge is applied at most twice per run and is logged as `/report.md missing after a final reply; nudging (n/2)` [1]. The report must be written in the current run: a report left by an earlier turn of a resumed thread does not count, but a run resumed from an interrupt accepts any existing report [1].

## Why it exists

Live `fireworks-glm` runs sometimes ended with the model announcing a delegation ("Let me delegate ...") in a reply with no tool call, which ended the run before the report was saved, leaving an empty report [1][3]. A prompt change alone ("never end the turn before `/report.md` is saved") did not stop this, so the `require_output` middleware was added as the fix (commit `8437852`), nudging the model back at most twice [3].

## Position and constraints

- In the canonical `STACK_ORDER` for YAML agents, `require_output` sits between `tool_retry` and `call_limit` [4]. Because it sits outside `call_limit`, the model calls that its nudges cause are counted against the run's call budget [4].
- Validation rejects a second enabled `require_output` in an agent's middleware list [4].

# The research agent's call and tool limits

## The budgets

- **Model calls (`call_limit`)**: a run stops after **60 model calls** for the orchestrator [1][2]. (The illustrative `agent.yaml` snippet in the docs shows `call_limit {max_model_calls: 40}` [3], but the description of the shipped Phase 1 standard stack and the README both state a 60-model-call budget [1][2].)
- **Tool calls (`tool_call_limit`)**: the orchestrator may call `web_search` **20 times** and `fetch_url` **25 times** per run [1][2]. When a budgeted tool is exhausted, further calls get an error tool message telling the model to stop [2]. Each `researcher` delegation gets its own budget of 30 model calls and 25 tool calls [1].
- These middleware limits — not the LangGraph recursion limit — are what actually bind a run; `run_config`'s recursion limit of 1000 is only a backstop [4]. `require_output` sits outside `call_limit`, so the model calls its nudges cause are counted against the budget [5].

## Why `write_file` is never budgeted

`write_file` is deliberately excluded from the tool-call budget so the report can always be saved [1][2]. This was learned the hard way: in Phase 1 recording attempt 2, the all-tools `tool_call_limit {run_limit: 40}` blocked the final `write_file` after 40 search/fetch calls, leaving two golden cases with empty reports. The fix (commit `c232712`) was to budget `web_search` (20) and `fetch_url` (25) individually and never budget `write_file` [6]. The agent's prompt reinforces this: if a tool reports its call limit, the model should stop gathering and write the report from what it has [7].

# What is `PlatformContext` and how is it passed to a run?

## What it is

`PlatformContext` is the frozen context object that **every run carries**; it is defined in `agentkit_core/context.py` [1]. It holds the identity fields that scope a run:

| Field | Type | Research CLI value |
|---|---|---|
| `tenant` | `Label` | `--tenant` (default `default`) |
| `product` | `Label` | `agentkit` (`PRODUCT`) |
| `team` | `Label` | `platform` (`TEAM`) |
| `user_id` | `Label`, not `global` | `--user` (default `local`) |
| `thread_id` | str | `--thread`, or a fresh uuid4 |
| `agent_name` | `Label` | the spec's `name` |
| `agent_version` | str | the spec's `version` |

[1]

The label fields follow the `Label` pattern `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,62}$` — lowercase, no dots (Postgres store namespaces reject dots, and labels become namespace parts), at most 63 characters. `check_label(value, what)` and `check_user_id(value)` raise `ValueError`, and the CLIs use them as argparse types so a bad value exits 2 before anything runs. `RESERVED_USER_IDS = {"global"}` reserves that name because `store_namespace` puts `"global"` in the owner slot for tenant-wide items, so a user named `global` would alias the tenant's namespace [1].

The context also feeds namespace construction: `store_namespace(ctx, scope, kind)` returns `(tenant, product, team, user_id if scope == "user" else "global", kind)` [1].

## How it is passed to a run

- **At invocation:** the context is passed on every graph call as `ainvoke(..., context=ctx)` or `astream(..., context=ctx)` [1].
- **At compile time:** agents built with `build_deep_agent` are compiled with `context_schema=PlatformContext`, so every run must pass `context=PlatformContext(...)` (a dict is validated against it) [2]. Flows do the same: `load_flow` compiles with `context_schema=PlatformContext` and is invoked with `context=PlatformContext(...)` (resuming an interrupt with `Command(resume={...})`) [3].
- **At runtime enforcement:** `TenantGuardMiddleware(deployment_tenant)` runs in `before_agent`. If there is no `PlatformContext` on the run it raises `MissingPlatformContext` ("agent runs need context=PlatformContext(...) on invoke/stream; got nothing"); if the run's tenant differs from the deployment tenant (from `AGENTKIT_TENANT`, default `default`) it raises `TenantMismatch` [4].
- **Downstream use:** `run_config` builds the run's `RunnableConfig` from the context — `configurable={"thread_id": ctx.thread_id}`, and metadata includes `tenant`, `product`, `team`, `user_id`, `thread_id`, `agent_name`, `agent_version` [5].

**Known gap:** `AgentSpec.name` is a plain string at validation time, so a name that is not a valid label passes `agentkit validate` and fails only when the CLI builds the `PlatformContext` [1].

# TenantGuardMiddleware: what it checks, and whether it isolates tenants

## What it checks

`TenantGuardMiddleware` is built around the deployment's tenant — `Settings.deployment_tenant`, read
from `AGENTKIT_TENANT` with a default of `default` — and runs in `before_agent` on every agent
invocation [1]. It checks two things on each run:

1. **That the run carries a `PlatformContext`.** If there is no `PlatformContext` on the run, it
   raises `MissingPlatformContext` ("agent runs need context=PlatformContext(...) on invoke/stream;
   got nothing") [1].
2. **That the run's tenant matches the deployment tenant.** If the run's tenant differs from the
   deployment's tenant, it raises `TenantMismatch` ("run tenant 'x' != deployment tenant 'y'") [1].

In the agent factory (`build_deep_agent`), the guard is always placed first: it is prepended to the
caller's middleware so the final list is `[guard, *middleware]`, and passing your own
`TenantGuardMiddleware` raises `ValueError` [2].

## Is it what isolates tenants?

**No.** The guard only *catches misrouted runs*; the isolation itself is the separate deployment [1].
Between tenants, isolation comes from each tenant having its own deployment: its own compose project
(`agentkit-<tenant>`) with its own Postgres database and volume, AES key, database password,
collector and ports — nothing is shared except the code and the model provider keys in the repo
`.env` [3][4]. `TenantGuardMiddleware` and the CLI pre-check are the runtime safety net that refuse
runs addressed to another tenant on top of that physical separation [5].

## Summary

- **Checks:** presence of `PlatformContext` (else `MissingPlatformContext`) and tenant match with the
  deployment tenant (else `TenantMismatch`) [1].
- **Isolation:** no — that is done by per-tenant deployments with separate infrastructure
  (database, volume, AES key, password, collector, ports); the middleware merely refuses misrouted
  runs [1][4].

# Giving a tenant its own deployment (a "tenant stamp")

## How to do it

Run one Make target — stamping requires Docker [1]:

```bash
make stamp TENANT=tenant-a
```

`make stamp` runs `scripts/stamp_tenant.sh <tenant>`, which [3]:

1. Validates the tenant name as a label and refuses the reserved name `example`.
2. On first use writes `deploy/tenants/<tenant>.env` (mode 600, git-ignored) containing a fresh 32-character `LANGGRAPH_AES_KEY`, a fresh database password, `DATABASE_URL`, and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`, plus two free host ports from 55500 upward (never 15432/16379 and never a port another tenant file holds; `STAMP_PG_PORT` and `STAMP_OTLP_PORT` can choose them explicitly). Later stamps reuse the file unchanged.
3. If the env file sets `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY` and `LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY`, configures the collector's exporters as `[file, otlp_http/langfuse]` (with `LANGFUSE_OTLP_ENDPOINT` and Basic `LANGFUSE_OTLP_AUTH`); otherwise just `[file]`.
4. Starts the stack with `docker compose -p agentkit-<tenant> --env-file deploy/tenants/<tenant>.env -f deploy/compose.yaml up -d --wait`.
5. Runs `scripts/tenant_setup.py`, which applies the checkpoint and store migrations and creates `agentkit_usage`.

To run workloads against that tenant, wrap commands with the tenant's env script — it exports `AGENTKIT_TENANT`, `DATABASE_URL`, `LANGGRAPH_AES_KEY` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` from the tenant file and runs your command (e.g. `scripts/tenant_env.sh tenant-a uv run research "question" --tenant tenant-a --persist`) [2][4]. It refuses to run if the repo `.env` sets `AGENTKIT_TENANT`, since `Settings` prefers `.env` and that would override every stamp [2]. Tear-down is `make unstamp TENANT=tenant-a` (`docker compose down -v` deletes the database but keeps the env file and key) [1].

## What the tenant gets

Each tenant gets its own fully isolated deployment — a dedicated compose project named `agentkit-<tenant>` — with its own Postgres (with its own named `pgdata` volume and generated password), its own always-on OpenTelemetry collector, its own host ports (`127.0.0.1:$AGENTKIT_PG_PORT` and `127.0.0.1:$AGENTKIT_OTLP_PORT`), its own database password and its own AES key. Nothing is shared between tenants except the code and the model provider keys in the repo `.env` [1][5][6]. Concretely:

- **Own containers, network, volume, host ports, database password, AES key and collector** [6].
- **Own trace sink:** the collector writes spans to `deploy/otel-out/<tenant>/spans.jsonl`, and optionally forwards to a Langfuse project when keys are set; traces carry the `agentkit.tenant` resource attribute and go only to that tenant's collector [5][7].
- **Isolation is enforced, not just conventional:** each deployment serves exactly one tenant (`Settings.deployment_tenant`, read from `AGENTKIT_TENANT`), and `TenantGuardMiddleware` rejects runs with no `PlatformContext` (`MissingPlatformContext`) or runs addressed to a different tenant (`TenantMismatch`) [8].
- **Verification:** `make phase0-exit` stamps `tenant-a` and `tenant-b` and proves they share no port or key, then asserts each collector file holds only its own tenant's spans and each database's `checkpoints.metadata` and `agentkit_usage` rows belong only to its tenant [9].

Two caveats: the env file `deploy/tenants/<tenant>.env` is the only copy of the tenant's AES key, so back it up [2]; and the stamp covers only the database, key, collector and ports — model provider keys still come from the shared repo `.env`, and items like an MCP gateway, OAuth vault, per-tenant model budgets and eval datasets are listed as a gap, not stamped [9].

# agentkit: what's encrypted at rest in Postgres vs. what stays plaintext

agentkit persists each tenant's threads and memory in encrypted Postgres, with each tenant getting its own stamped deployment (own database and AES key) [2][3]. Encryption uses `LANGGRAPH_AES_KEY` with a `msgpack+aes` serializer [1][4].

## Encrypted at rest

Encrypted with `LANGGRAPH_AES_KEY` [1]:

- **`checkpoint_blobs`** – container state channels: `messages`, `files` (including `/report.md`), `selection`, `todos`, and other lists/dicts, stored as msgpack+aes blobs [1].
- **`checkpoint_writes`** – pending writes, also msgpack+aes [1].
- **Store item values** – memory items in `store.value`, encrypted by `EncryptedStore` into `{"__enc": "<type>+aes", "ct": "<base64>"}` envelopes using the same serializer and key as the checkpoints, and decrypted on get and search [1][4].

## Stays plaintext

- **`checkpoints.checkpoint`** – primitive top-level state channels (str, int, float, bool) are stored inline as JSONB, not encrypted [1].
- **`checkpoints.metadata`** – run metadata (tenant, user_id, thread_id, agent, prompt_hash, step) as plaintext JSONB, because LangGraph copies string run metadata there [1].
- **Store namespaces, keys, timestamps, TTLs** – left plaintext so prefix search, `list_namespaces` and the TTL sweeper work [1][4].
- **`agentkit_usage`** – the usage ledger holds only identifiers and token counts per run, unencrypted [1].
- **`checkpoint_migrations`, `store_migrations`** – migration bookkeeping tables [1].

## Notes on EncryptedStore behavior

`EncryptedStore` wraps the inner store and refuses a search with a value `filter`, rejects an inner store with a vector index, and raises `StoreEncryptionError` for any stored value that is not an encryption envelope — a plaintext value is never returned [4]. Postgres contracts in the test suite verify that an encrypted round trip leaves no plaintext in blobs [5].

# Why agentkit wraps a turn in `thread_lock`

`thread_lock` serializes a whole turn against other runs on the same thread:

```python
async with thread_lock(p, thread_id):
    ...  # one turn
```

## The reason

It holds a Postgres advisory lock — `pg_advisory_lock(hashtext(thread_id))` — taken on a connection from a dedicated lock pool for the duration of the turn [1]. The purpose is to prevent two concurrent runs on the same thread from **forking the checkpoint chain and losing an update**; the docs note that a Postgres contract pins both the failure mode and this fix [1].

## Design details

- **Separate lock pool.** The lock comes from its own connection pool, so a run waiting on a lock cannot starve the checkpointer/saver of connections [1].
- **`hashtext` collisions are harmless.** Because `hashtext` is 32-bit, two *different* threads can rarely map to the same lock key. In that case the runs are merely serialized (one waits for the other); no correctness issue arises [1].
- **Persistence is the precondition.** Without `--persist` there is no database and no lock at all (`--thread`/resume is rejected), so the lock only exists in the persistent mode where checkpoints are shared [2].

# Pruning old threads

## How to prune

Run the prune command with an age cutoff:

```bash
uv run agentkit-prune --older-than 30d     # also 12h, 45m
```

The accepted age units include days (`30d`), hours (`12h`) and minutes (`45m`) [1].

Internally, `prune(persistence, older_than)` selects threads whose newest checkpoint `ts` is older than the cutoff and deletes each one with `saver.adelete_thread`, which removes the thread's checkpoints, blobs and writes [1]. On success it prints `pruned N threads`; a bad age or configuration prints a single line and exits with status 2 [1].

## What pruning leaves behind

Pruning deletes threads only. Specifically, it does **not** touch:

- **Store items** — memory items stored in the store survive pruning. A notable case: `research-eval --persist` creates a fresh `eval-<hex>` user per invocation, and those users' (encrypted) store items are never pruned, since `agentkit-prune` deletes threads only [1][2][3].
- **`agentkit_usage` rows** — usage/billing records for the pruned threads remain [1].

Two operational caveats:

- Prune has **no tenant filter**; this is safe only while each tenant has its own database, and a tenant filter is needed if tenants ever share one [1][3].
- Memory-item expiry is a separate concern: `STORE_DEFAULT_TTL_MINUTES` is unset by default, so store items never expire unless configured [3].

# What does the CostLedger record and does it store prices?

## What it records

`CostLedger(persistence=None)` is an async callback handler that tracks per-run token usage [1]. Specifically, it:

- Maps every callback run id to its root run [1].
- Sums `usage_metadata` from `on_llm_end` — input tokens, output tokens, and cached input tokens (from `input_token_details.cache_read`) [1].
- Records model names from `ls_model_name` [1].
- Adds Decisions tokens from the `agentkit.decisions_usage` custom event [1].

When the root run ends, it appends one `UsageRow` with the fields `tenant`, `thread_id`, `run_id`, `model`, `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cached_input_tokens`, `decisions_input_tokens`, and `decisions_output_tokens` [1]. A run with no model call and no selection — for example, one the guard refused — writes no row [1]. Its `summary()` method produces the one-line `usage:` total shown by the CLIs [1].

With persistence enabled, each row is also inserted into the `agentkit_usage` table (`on conflict (run_id) do nothing`); `setup(persistence)` creates the table and the `(tenant, created_at)` index idempotently inside one transaction under an advisory lock. A failed insert only logs a warning and never fails the run [1].

## Does it store prices?

No. Despite its name, the ledger stores tokens only — there is no price table and no money amount [1].

# When is tracing on, and what is masked in spans by default?

## When tracing is on

Tracing is **off** unless the environment variable `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set [1]. When the run starts, the CLI enters `research_agent.telemetry.tracing(Settings())`, which calls `configure_tracing` with the deployment tenant — and it stays off without that endpoint variable [3]. When enabled, `configure_tracing` builds an `OTLPSpanExporter` posting to `<endpoint>/v1/traces` (OTLP over HTTP, `export_timeout_seconds` default 2 s), creates its own `TracerProvider` (not the global one) with resource attributes `service.name` (from `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME`, default `agentkit`) and `agentkit.tenant`, and binds a `Langfuse` client to it; spans go only to the collector, which may forward to Langfuse. `LANGSMITH_TRACING` is never set because LangSmith's OTel path has no masking hook [1].

## What is masked in spans by default

Masking is the default; setting `AGENTKIT_TRACE_PAYLOADS=1` turns it off [2]. By default:

- **Prompt and completion attributes**: `mask_payloads` deletes `langfuse.observation.input`, `langfuse.observation.output`, `langfuse.trace.input`, `langfuse.trace.output`, and every attribute starting with `gen_ai.prompt`, `gen_ai.completion`, `gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages`, or `gen_ai.system_instructions`; a masked span is marked with `agentkit.payload.masked = true` [2].
- **Error status message attribute**: `langfuse.observation.status_message` is kept only if it fully matches `[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*(Error|Exception|Exit|Interrupt|Cancelled|Mismatch)`; anything else (e.g. an error tool message's content) becomes `redacted` [2].
- **Langfuse error hook**: `MaskingCallbackHandler` records errors as `type(error).__name__` instead of `str(error)` [2].
- **Span status description and exception events**: `redact_errors` (in the exporter) keeps the status description only if it is an exception type name recorded in the span's `exception.type` events or shaped like one, otherwise falls back to a type-shaped status attribute, otherwise `redacted`; exception events lose `exception.message`, `exception.stacktrace`, and `exception.escaped`, keeping only `exception.type` [2].

# Gating a change against the golden baseline

## How to gate

Run `research-eval` with `--gate` pointed at the gates file, which compares your run against the committed baseline (`apps/research_agent/evals/baseline.json`) [1]:

```bash
uv run research-eval --model fireworks-glm --dataset apps/research_agent/evals/golden.jsonl \
  --judge anthropic --gate apps/research_agent/evals/gates.yaml [--write-baseline] --out <file.md>
```

What the gate checks, and when:

- The `gates.yaml` file names the baseline (path relative to itself), a `min_cases` floor, and per-metric bounds: `min`, `max`, `max_drop` (absolute drop from the baseline) and `max_rise` (relative rise, e.g. `0.30` = +30%) [1].
- The comparison happens **after** the run, so even a mismatched gate run still costs its (full-set) cases [1].
- The gate **fails** when a metric breaks its bounds, a metric is missing, there are fewer than `min_cases` cases, or a case that completed in the baseline now errors [1].
- It **refuses to compare** (a "mismatch") when the dataset bytes (SHA-256), the agent `model_id` or the judge `model_id` differ from the baseline — in that case, re-record the baseline instead [1].
- `--write-baseline` (requires `--gate`) writes a new baseline from the current run, and refuses if any case errored [1].
- The gate needs the full case set: `--case` / `--tag` subsets are **not** allowed with `--gate` [3].

For reference, the committed golden baseline gates are [2]:

| Metric | Gate |
|---|---|
| completed | min 0.96 |
| has_citation | min 0.96 |
| sources_section | min 0.90 |
| source_count_ok | (not gated) |
| citation_validity | min 0.85, max_drop 0.05 |
| completeness | min 0.85, max_drop 0.05 |
| groundedness | min 0.55, max_drop 0.10 |
| tool_recall | min 0.90 |
| mean_latency_s | (not gated) |
| mean_total_tokens | max_rise 0.30 |

## Exit codes

| Exit | Meaning | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Gate passed, or baseline written | `gate: PASS` / `gate: baseline written to <path>` |
| **1** | Regression — including NaN scores, and baseline cases that are missing from or errored in the run | one `gate: FAIL <metric>: <detail>` line per failure |
| **2** | No baseline, unreadable baseline, mismatch, or errored cases on `--write-baseline` | `gate: no baseline at ...`, `gate: unreadable baseline ...`, `gate: baseline mismatch: ...`, `gate: refusing to write baseline, cases errored: [...]` |

Every `gate:` line except `PASS` and `baseline written` goes to **stderr** [1].

Observed examples from the project's own verification: a deliberately weakened prompt run with `--gate` exited 1 with `gate: FAIL` on has_citation (0.00), sources_section (0.00), citation_validity (0.00, min and max_drop), groundedness (0.03) and tool_recall (0.00); a dataset judged with a mismatched judge model printed `gate: baseline mismatch: baseline dataset_sha256 mismatch: ...; re-record the baseline`, exited 2, and left `baseline.json` unchanged [2].

# Why the first Phase 1 baseline attempt failed with `GraphRecursionError` — and the fix

## What happened

The first recording attempt produced **11 × `GraphRecursionError`** plus 1 empty report — only 13 of the
25 golden cases completed [1].

## Root cause

The `run_config` builder set the LangGraph **recursion limit to 100**. But in this DeepAgents stack,
**every middleware `before_model`/`after_model` hook counts as its own graph step** — the standard stack
costs about **nine graph steps per model call**. With a limit of 100, runs died after roughly **eleven
model calls**, which is far too few for a research task, so most runs hit `GraphRecursionError`
mid-investigation [1][2][3].

## The fix

The recursion limit was raised to **1000 (commit `7d33de5`)** — but explicitly reframed as a **backstop,
not the run's budget** [1][2]. The actual spending limits are enforced by the `call_limit` and
`tool_call_limit` middleware (e.g., `run_config(ctx, prompt_hash, ledger, *, recursion_limit=1000)` is the
one place that sets this, and the CLIs get it from there; flow agent nodes invoke without a config and keep
LangGraph's default of 9,999) [2][3].

## Outcome

Attempt 2 then failed differently (2 empty reports because the all-tools `tool_call_limit {run_limit: 40}`
blocked the final `write_file`), which led to per-tool budgets (`web_search` 20, `fetch_url` 25, never
`write_file`, commit `c232712`). After further prompt and middleware fixes, attempt 4 completed 25/25 and
wrote the baseline, later superseded by attempt 6 (25/25, first recording with the `## Sources` prompt and
`require_output`) [1].

# Risk T9 found with Decisions selection and a vague system prompt

**The risk:** with a vague system prompt, the Decisions-based tool selection hides (drops) every tool, leaving the agent unable to search [1][2].

## Details

- T9 (Phase 0) tested the research agent end to end with `selection: decisions` and passed on 2026-11-02 [3]. As part of it, two real `/v1/decisions` responses (model `gpt-6-luna`, HTTP 200) were recorded and kept as test fixtures (`decisions_live_orchestrator.json`, `decisions_live_short_prompt.json`) [1][2].
- With the **real orchestrator prompt**, `web_search` and `fetch_url` scored 1.00 each (kept, since tools are kept at probability ≥ 0.5), and the irrelevant `sql` tool scored 0.00 (dropped) [1].
- With the **one-line vague prompt "You are a deep-research agent."**, `web_search` scored 0.03 and `fetch_url` 0.01 — far below the 0.5 threshold — so the agent would have lost search entirely [2][4]. (That prompt also made Decisions pick the "fast" tier with 0.97 confidence, whereas the real prompt kept the default tier because its 0.27 confidence was below the 0.5 floor [1].)

## Mitigation / status

- Agents using `selection: decisions` need a system prompt that says which tools to use and when [1][2].
- A "minimum tools" guard was **not** implemented; it is only a candidate for the ToolSurface work in Phase 3 [1][4].
